problem: Mobile robots in unstructured, human-populated areas struggle to plan safe paths, and existing person-following methods let the robot sway around the leader rather than reproduce the leader's exact path. They also rarely combine re-identification of a specific person with online learning.
motivation: Safety and regulation constraints block deployment of heavy robots in shared spaces. Delegating motion planning to a human who walks the route (teach-by-showing) removes the need for complex planning and sensing. This needs robust identification of one specific leader, even through occlusions, crowds and exits from the camera view.
key_idea: A human leader walks the path, and the robot re-identifies and tracks the leader using CNN features with KNN, camera-LIDAR fusion and a multiple-model Kalman filter, then reconstructs the footsteps as a smooth clothoid path to follow.
insight: Combining a learned appearance recogniser (GoogLeNet features + online-updated KNN) with LIDAR fusion and motion-model filtering lets the system keep tracking the leader when vision fails, for example in sharp turns. Backbone choice matters: GoogLeNet features gave over 90% correct KNN responses on Market1501 against about 50% for ResNet50. The OptiTrack comparison shows the followed path within ±25 cm of the human footsteps. These results are qualitative and reported for single runs, not as an ablation.
method: Detection: SSD (MobileNet) detects people in each frame, with YOLOv3 also mentioned. The person with the largest bounding box at start becomes the leader, and a drift-tolerance radius d = t·s·(w/100)^2 rejects detections far from the last known leader position.

Recognition: KNN over GoogLeNet (1024-d) or ResNet50 (2048-d) features. It is initialised with leader crops and negatives from a customised Market1501, then continuously updated with new leader points and negative detections during following.
Image tracker: KCF, CSRT or MOSSE tracks the leader for m frames between detection/recognition passes for speed.

LIDAR-camera fusion: LIDAR points are clustered into object centroids, and bounding-box centroids are lifted to 3D using RealSense depth. A finite-state spatio-temporal correspondence algorithm matches them in the local frame, with ego-motion compensation, so either sensor alone suffices.

Global human tracking: two Kalman filters (constant-velocity KF and unicycle EKF) are combined with a first-order generalised pseudo-Bayesian multiple-model estimator. It tracks the leader in the world frame using an a-priori map and localisation, and continues while the leader is outside the camera view.
Path reconstruction: leader positions are recorded when they move more than a threshold, smoothed with LOESS, resampled at uniform curvilinear distance, and interpolated with a G2 clothoid spline.

Robot control: velocity-independent path following (Andreetto et al.) with speed set by distance to the leader, path curvature and past velocities. Obstacles trigger slow-down then stop, and a sound is emitted if the leader gets too far.

setting.backbone: SSD/MobileNet detector + GoogLeNet features with KNN (pretrained CNN, online KNN) + Kalman filters; no LLM
setting.training_data: Pretrained CNN classifiers; KNN is trained online on leader crops collected during initialisation, with negatives from a customised Market1501 dataset
setting.observation: RGB-D (RealSense D435) + 360° 2D LIDAR (RPLidar A3) + wheel encoders / RealSense T265 visual odometry
setting.action_space: continuous unicycle velocity commands (linear and angular) along a clothoid path
setting.privileged: A-priori map of the environment and a global localisation system are used to estimate robot pose in the world frame; OptiTrack (8 cameras) used only for ground-truth evaluation

numbers_note: No standard navigation benchmark is used. Results are qualitative real-robot trajectories, an FPS table for trackers and KNN recognition accuracy on Market1501 (ResNet50 about 50%, GoogLeNet over 90%).
results: In real hallway experiments the robot kept following the correct leader with another pedestrian nearby, and recovered the leader after sharp turns using LIDAR. Against OptiTrack ground truth, the robot's trajectory stayed within ±25 cm of the human footsteps. Tracker speeds: MOSSE 56 FPS, KCF 38, CSRT 15.
limitations: A leader misclassified as a mismatch cannot be re-evaluated, and repeated failures force the robot to stop and reinitialise from scratch.
Requires a prior map and global localisation, and evaluation is qualitative with no large-scale quantitative comparison to baselines.
Tracker and detector choices are tuned empirically and evaluation covers only a single indoor hallway environment.
